name: Vihta / venik whisking

lead: A venik (Russian) or vihta/vasta (Finnish) is a bundle of leafy birch, oak or eucalyptus branches that bathers use in a steam bath to whisk and lightly slap the skin. The tradition says it gets the skin flushed, stimulates the pores and makes the skin feel soft and clean, which is the appearance appeal for people who add it to a skincare or wellness routine.

The practice comes from Russian banya and Finnish sauna culture and is mainly a social and sensory ritual. Studies on sauna bathing in general exist, but no published study has examined whisking for skin appearance.

paras: In a banya the dried bundle is soaked in very hot water, then used after the first sweat to wave hot air over the body and to pat or stroke the skin; in summer some people use fresh or frozen-and-thawed bundles. Bathers usually alternate heat with cool-down breaks, and felt hats protect the head from heat.

Sauna conditions bring documented risks: dehydration, alcohol and heat together raise the risk of sudden death, and people with unstable angina or severe aortic stenosis are advised against sauna bathing. Hot surfaces cause burns, and those with high blood pressure or diabetes are generally advised to keep sessions shorter.

angle.text: People use the bundle to get a flushed, fresh look and a smooth feel to the skin after a steam session. The skin benefit is a traditional claim rather than a measured outcome.

lead: A venik is a bundle of leafy branches, typically white birch, oak or eucalyptus, used in the Russian banya to massage the body and to move hot air around it [1]. The Finnish equivalent, the vihta or vasta, is a bundle of birch twigs with fresh leaves used to lightly slap the skin [2].

Bathers say the whisking stimulates the pores and cells and leaves the skin flushed and refreshed [2]. In looksmaxxing and lifestyle circles it is mentioned as a skin-and-circulation ritual alongside sauna and cold plunge.

Research on sauna use is broader than the whisking itself: Finnish-style sauna is associated with lower cardiovascular risk, while evidence for skin disorders is described as insufficient [2]. No studies of whisking for appearance were found.

paras: The Russian banny venik is made of dried branches and leaves, moistened with very hot water before use; in summer, fresh bundles are sometimes used or frozen and thawed [1]. It is generally first used during the second sweat, though some bathers wait until the third [1]. It helps transfer heat from the air to the body and doubles as a massage tool [1]. A birch besom appears in a 1926 painting by Boris Kustodiev, illustrating its place in Russian culture [1]. In Finland the vihta is a bundle of birch twigs used to lightly slap the skin [2].

Traditional accounts say whisking stimulates pores and cells and promotes circulation and a clean, soft skin feel [2]. Banya temperatures often exceed 93 degrees C, and bathers wear felt or wool hats to protect the head and hair [1].

Sauna guidance notes that alcohol, dehydration or narcotics while bathing raise the risk of sudden death; people who are severely obese or have high blood pressure or diabetes should keep sessions shorter; sauna is contraindicated for unstable angina and severe aortic stenosis; pregnant women are advised to keep core temperature at or below 39.0 degrees C; and stove burns and hot metal jewellery are hazards [2].

No studies found. Studies of sauna bathing in general associate long-term Finnish sauna use with lower risk of sudden cardiac death and report tentative evidence for blood pressure and arterial stiffness, but describe evidence for skin disorders as insufficient [2].
